applicable_when: The kernel is a transpose: it reads in_ptr0 with a stride-128 (512-byte) step along the x-dimension (y0 + 128*x2 + 4032000*y1), making loads non-coalesced. Each warp issues 32 separate 32-byte sector requests instead of a single 128-byte transaction. This saturates L2 (97% throughput) and causes 44.3-cycle average L1TEX stall per warp (58.8% of all stall cycles). L1 hit rate is 0%, meaning every load goes to L2/DRAM. Adding tl.max_contiguous and tl.multiple_of hints on the load index tells the Triton compiler that the x-dimension index is contiguous and aligned, enabling it to emit 128-bit (float4) vectorized loads instead of scalar 32-bit loads. This reduces the number of memory transactions by 4x for the x-dimension, relieving L2 pressure and reducing per-warp stall cycles.

applicable_when: The kernel performs a strided transpose: input stride is (4032000,1,32000,128) channels-last while output is contiguous. With XBLOCK=128 and YBLOCK=8, each thread in a warp loads from addresses separated by 128 elements (512 bytes), producing 32 distinct cache lines per warp load — maximally non-coalesced. This causes 0% L1 hit rate and 97% L2 utilization. The fix is to swap the tile orientation so that the YBLOCK dimension (which has stride-1 in the load: y0 = yindex % 128) is the fast-moving dimension across threads, making loads coalesced. Using YBLOCK=128 with XBLOCK=1 means adjacent threads differ only in y0, which maps to consecutive memory addresses (stride 1 in in_ptr0). Adding @triton.autotune explores the best tile shape automatically.
